title: ICA says NSW committee backing lifts insurance levy reform
full_text:
A bipartisan NSW parliamentary committee has unanimously recommended replacing the state’s Emergency Services Levy (ESL), and the Insurance Council of Australia (ICA) says the finding means reform now has support from across the NSW Parliament.
The Select Committee on Emergency Services Funding Reform, chaired by independent MP Jacqui Scruby and comprising three government, three opposition and two crossbench members, backed a fairer model for funding emergency services. The ICA’s Wednesday statement welcomed the result.
The levy added up to 34% to insurance costs before GST and stamp duty in the last financial year, with customers paying more than $1.5 billion through it. The ICA argues those without cover contribute nothing towards emergency services the whole community relies on, and that extreme weather and construction cost inflation are already pushing premiums higher and more people towards underinsurance.
ICA chief executive Andrew Hall welcomed the finding.
“The current NSW Parliament has acknowledged that every household and business in the state have been taxed for doing the right thing by taking out insurance for far too long,” Hall said.
Read more: Emergency services levy reform wins unanimous committee backing
Hall said the next government should act early.
“Whoever forms government after March, the people of New South Wales should be confident that both sides of politics now agree this tax is unfair and must go, and the next parliament needs to make delivering a fairer way to fund emergency services an early priority,” he said.
The ICA wants all parties to commit to legislating the reform early in the next term and says it stands ready to work with the incoming government on a fair and orderly transition.
Hall noted that One Nation had also committed to removing taxes from insurance, adding to bipartisan support. He said the burden falls hardest on communities exposed to bushfire, flood and storm, along with small businesses, strata owners, renters and families on tight budgets.
“Removing this tax is unfinished business, and every year it stays in place is another year people are paying more than they should to protect their homes and livelihoods,” he said.
Read more: NSW brokers face a premium gap that policy, not risk, created
A committee recommendation is not legislation. As of August, the government had not identified a preferred model among five Treasury options. NSW Treasury modelling estimates the average replacement levy for insured homes would be $65 lower under all five options, and independent modelling has estimated that stripping the ESL from premiums could expand the insured base by about 400,000 policies.
The Minns Government says it wants a simple and transparent levy spread across all properties. The National Insurance Brokers Association (NIBA) has long opposed the insurance-based levy, warning that the current system adds pressure to premiums at a time when affordability is already under strain, and has advised brokers to follow the process closely given potential impacts on pricing, client communication and product placement.
For brokers working with clients in regional communities and exposed to natural hazards, strata owners and small businesses, the ESL reform has the most direct stakes. The March election and the new parliament’s early agenda will determine whether this recommendation becomes legislation or follows the path of the Berejiklian government’s 2017 deferral, when insurers and brokers spent a year preparing before reform was shelved.
